title: Markov chains
subtitle: Tomorrow depends only on today. That single assumption predicts weather, web rankings and queue lengths.

def.title: The Markov property
def.body: A Markov chain moves between states; the probability of the next state depends only on the current state, not on how it got there. The chain is described by a transition matrix P where Pij is the probability of going from i to j and each row sums to 1. Example: Sunny → Sunny 0.9, Sunny → Rainy 0.1, Rainy → Sunny 0.5, Rainy → Rainy 0.5.

evolve.title: Evolving the distribution
evolve.body: If π₀ is the starting distribution (a row vector), then π₁ = π₀P, π₂ = π₁P, … The probabilities of each state after n steps are the entries of πₙ. Starting sunny: π₀ = (1, 0); π₁ = (0.9, 0.1); π₂ = (0.86, 0.14).
evolve.steps: π₁ = π₀P with π₀ = (1, 0). π₂ = π₁P.

steady.title: Steady state
steady.body: For most chains the distribution converges to a steady state π satisfying π = πP, regardless of the start. Solve π(1−0.9) = 0.5π₂ ⇒ 0.1π₁ = 0.5π₂ ⇒ π₁ = 5π₂, and π₁ + π₂ = 1, so π = (5/6, 1/6) = (0.8333, 0.1667): in the long run it is sunny 83% of days. The simulation shows convergence from a sunny start.

types.title: Kinds of state
types.body: A state is absorbing if once entered it is never left (Pii = 1) — a game’s “ruined” state. A chain is irreducible if every state can reach every other; periodic if returns happen only at multiples of some period. Irreducible, aperiodic chains are ergodic: they have a unique steady state.

app.title: Applications
app.body: Weather and text generation, PageRank (a random surfer on the web graph has a steady state that ranks pages), queues (the number in an M/M/1 queue is a birth–death chain), reliability (working/failed states), genetics, finance and speech recognition (hidden Markov models).
app.steps: A machine is Up or Down. Up → Down 0.1, Down → Up 0.6. Steady state: 0.1π_Up = 0.6π_Down ⇒ π_Up = 6π_Down, so π_Up = 6/7.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Next state depends on the current state only; π ← πP.
  • Ergodic chains have a unique steady state π = πP.
